categories.label: Absence and Applicability of Standard/Model Contracts for MMC
categories.memo: Covers the fundamental gap identified across studies: standard construction contract forms (CCDC, FIDIC, NEC, AIA, ConsensusDocs) were not designed with MMC/prefabrication/modular construction in mind, and no dedicated standard forms exist for this delivery method, forcing adaptation of conventional forms.

codes.label: No dedicated standard contract exists for MMC/MOC
codes.description: Studies note the complete absence of standard contract forms specifically developed for modular/off-site construction, forcing parties to adapt conventional COC-based contracts (e.g., CCDC) to MMC projects.

codes.label: Untested suitability of risk-sharing based standard forms for MiC
codes.description: Standard forms like FIDIC and NEC are built on established risk-sharing philosophies, but literature has not assessed whether these allocations are appropriate for MiC/MMC projects.

codes.label: Recycling/reuse of templates without adequate modification
codes.description: Practitioners often reuse contract templates from prior projects with insufficient tailoring to MMC needs, perpetuating ambiguity and misfit.

codes.label: Insufficient MOC-specific specifications
codes.description: Modular/off-site construction lacks separate, adequate technical specifications compared to conventional construction, compounding contractual ambiguity.

categories.label: Payment Mechanisms and Financial Provisions for Off-Site Production
categories.memo: Focuses on how standard contract payment clauses (progress payments, advance payments, valuation of completed work) are structured around on-site, work-done measurement and fail to accommodate off-site manufacturing, upfront financing needs, and module ownership/transfer issues.

codes.label: Progress payment clauses tied to on-site completion
codes.description: Standard payment clauses (e.g., CCDC 14 §5.2.3) measure completion via on-site inspection, which is incompatible with MMC where most value is created off-site in factories.

codes.label: Need to shift from 'work done' to 'work due' payment logic
codes.description: MMC requires payment mechanisms recognizing fabrication progress and milestones rather than only physical installation on site.

codes.label: Ambiguous definition of 'Products'/materials for prefabricated modules
codes.description: Standard contract definitions of incorporated materials/products do not clearly extend to off-site fabricated modules, creating disputes over claimable payment for undelivered/uninstalled modules.

codes.label: Advance payment and upfront financing needs unaddressed
codes.description: MMC requires greater upfront capital for materials/fabrication, but standard contracts lack clear provisions for adjusting advance payments accordingly.

codes.label: Retention and liquidated damages provisions misaligned with MMC risk profile
codes.description: MMC contractors commonly seek removal/reduction of retention and liquidated damages clauses that do not reflect off-site production realities.

codes.label: Payment security amid supplier insolvency risk
codes.description: Heightened insolvency risk among specialist MMC suppliers raises concerns about existing payment security provisions in standard forms.

codes.label: Unclear payment terms as leading litigation driver in MOC
codes.description: Empirical court case analysis shows unclear payment terms are the dominant cause of disputes in MOC projects compared to other issue types.

categories.label: Variation and Change Management Provisions
categories.memo: Addresses how standard contract clauses governing variations, changes, and value engineering are structured, and whether they adequately support MMC's fixed early design and off-site fabrication constraints.

codes.label: Variation procedures unsuited to fixed/early MMC design
codes.description: Early design freeze in MMC conflicts with standard variation order procedures designed for flexible, evolving on-site design changes.

codes.label: Valuation methods for variations
codes.description: Clear valuation methods for pricing variations are identified as the most critical clause for fairness and dispute minimization, with sole-discretion valuation by employer/engineer favoring employer interests.

codes.label: Scope limitation and contractor's right to decline variations
codes.description: Absence of limitation clauses on variation scope, or of contractor rights to decline unreasonable variations, increases risk of disputes and uncompensated secondary impacts.

codes.label: Change-in-law and notification/time-bar provisions
codes.description: Absence of change-in-law clauses and varying notification/time-bar requirements across contract forms (e.g., NEC compensation events) affect proactive risk management of variations.

codes.label: Value engineering benefit-sharing clauses
codes.description: How cost/benefit from contractor-initiated value engineering is allocated between employer and contractor affects contractor motivation to propose efficiency improvements relevant to MMC innovation.

codes.label: Legal tradition shaping variation clause clarity
codes.description: Civil-law-influenced FIDIC clauses provide more descriptive variation guidance than common-law-influenced AIA/NEC forms, affecting clarity and risk allocation.

categories.label: Risk Allocation and Liability Structures
categories.memo: Covers how standard contracts distribute risk and liability between owner and contractor, including transportation risk, design liability shifts, and the balance/imbalance created by general and particular conditions.

codes.label: Unaddressed transportation and module-specific risk/insurance
codes.description: Standard contracts lack clear provisions for care-of-works and insurance coverage during transportation of prefabricated modules, and do not extend coverage to off-site storage.

codes.label: Design liability shift to manufacturers/suppliers
codes.description: MMC shifts design and engineering responsibility to manufacturers, but existing contracts fail to reflect this altered liability structure or require shared design liability from early contractor/supplier involvement.

codes.label: Employer-driven bias and unilateral drafting of risk clauses
codes.description: Standard contracts are typically drafted unilaterally by owners and are further modified during tendering to shift risk toward contractors, often removing contractor-favorable clauses.

codes.label: Risk-matching principle and imbalance in obligations across objectives
codes.description: Risk should be allocated to the party best able to manage it; empirical clause analysis shows obligations are more fairly shared for cost/schedule than for quality, safety, and environmental objectives.

codes.label: Effect of particular/bespoke conditions on general risk balance
codes.description: Particular conditions add detail and complexity (mostly through supplementary clarifying sentences) but generally do not fundamentally alter the risk-mitigation balance set by general conditions, though excessive amendment of contingency clauses is riskier than coordination clause amendments.

codes.label: External and jurisdictional risk factors specific to MOC
codes.description: Transportation restrictions, contradictory cross-jurisdictional regulations, lack of a modular building code, and local industry maturity are MOC-specific risk factors poorly captured in current contract risk allocation, though rarely observed in actual litigation.

codes.label: Disclaimer clauses and cost impact of unbalanced risk transfer
codes.description: Contractual disclaimer clauses transferring unpredictable risk to one party can raise contract costs substantially and negatively affect tendering and relationships.

categories.label: Termination, Suspension, Dispute Resolution and Liability Limitation Clauses
categories.memo: Addresses how standard/IPD contract forms structure termination rights, suspension procedures, dispute escalation, and liability caps, and how ambiguity in these clauses drives disputes.

codes.label: Ambiguity in suspension and termination rights
codes.description: Lack of clarity regarding parties' rights and obligations upon suspension or termination is a recurring source of costly disputes.

codes.label: Divergent termination procedures across standard forms
codes.description: Standard forms differ in the discretion and notice requirements they give owners for termination, with some forms placing other parties at a disadvantage.

codes.label: Tiered dispute resolution and mediation requirements
codes.description: IPD and other standard contracts often require internal escalation and mediation before binding arbitration or litigation, aiming to reduce dispute costs.

codes.label: Liability limitation and waiver provisions
codes.description: Standard forms differ substantially in how they cap or waive liability for claims and damages, affecting risk distribution between parties.

codes.label: Cost-inefficiency of pursuing contractual claims/disputes
codes.description: Dispute resolution processes can generate costs exceeding amounts recovered, underscoring the importance of efficient clause design.

categories.label: Delivery Method and Procurement Structures Enabling MMC
categories.memo: Concerns how project delivery method selection (DBB, DB, CM, IPD) interacts with standard contract forms to support or hinder early contractor/supplier involvement, collaboration, and MMC-specific coordination needs.

codes.label: Design-Build and Construction Management favored over DBB
codes.description: DB and CM delivery methods are recommended and empirically shown to be more cost-effective for MMC/MiC due to earlier contractor involvement in design, compared to traditional DBB.

codes.label: Absence of identified best-practice delivery method for MiC
codes.description: Despite recognition that early contractor involvement is essential, literature has not established a definitive best project delivery method for MiC across contexts.

codes.label: IPD/multi-party contracts as promising but under-researched for DfMA/MMC
codes.description: Multi-party IPD contracts (e.g., CCDC30, AIA C-191, ConsensusDocs 300) with shared risk/reward and joint decision-making better support DfMA/MMC collaboration than traditional fragmented forms, but remain understudied.

codes.label: Traditional contract fragmentation as barrier to DfMA/MMC
codes.description: Design-bid-build and other traditional delivery structures create vertical/horizontal/longitudinal fragmentation and information silos that obstruct the integration DfMA/MMC requires.

codes.label: Two-stage procurement and early supply chain engagement
codes.description: Two-stage procurement approaches and early supply chain/manufacturer involvement are favored in MMC contexts to balance cost certainty with client risk aversion.

codes.label: Dominance of standard forms despite misfit, due to familiarity
codes.description: Standard forms remain dominant in MMC procurement mainly due to stakeholder familiarity, simplicity, and proven workability rather than genuine suitability, with JCT favored for its amendability.

categories.label: Roles, Responsibilities and Scope Definition Gaps
categories.memo: Covers how standard contracts fail to clearly define stakeholder roles, scope of work, and manufacturer relationships relevant to MMC/DfMA, contributing to duplication, confusion, and disputes.

codes.label: Unclear stakeholder roles and responsibilities
codes.description: Contracts often lack clearly defined roles and responsibilities among the expanded set of stakeholders (manufacturers, suppliers, contractors) involved in DfMA/MMC projects.

codes.label: Ambiguous scope of work causing duplication and confusion
codes.description: Lack of clear scope-of-work definition in contracts leads to duplication and confusion among project participants engaged in prefabrication.

codes.label: Lack of reference to multiple manufacturers
codes.description: Contracts do not adequately provide for sourcing flexibility across multiple prefabrication manufacturers, limiting supply chain adaptability.

codes.label: Contractual relationships between MiC participants unexamined
codes.description: There is a broad absence of literature and contract content addressing how contractual relationships among diverse MiC participants (manufacturer, contractor, designer, owner) should be structured.

categories.label: Emerging Technology and Regulatory Gaps in Contract Frameworks
categories.memo: Addresses how standard contracts fail to address BIM, digital DfMA platforms, and broader legislative/regulatory frameworks needed to support MMC implementation.

codes.label: Absence of standard BIM contract forms and liability clarity
codes.description: No standard contract form exists to address BIM implementation, liability for design errors/data misuse, or insurance applicable to BIM, constraining adoption relevant to MMC's digital design/manufacturing workflows.

codes.label: Misalignment between DfMA digital platforms and standard contracts
codes.description: DfMA-supporting digital platforms are not well aligned with existing standard contracts such as CCDC forms, limiting integration of digital workflows into contractual processes.

codes.label: Lack of legislative/regulatory frameworks for DfMA/MMC
codes.description: Absence of specific codes, guidelines, and standards for DfMA/MMC implementation hampers systematic contractual adoption, and public procurement frameworks disadvantage innovative MMC firms.
